en.title: Kayumars, the First King
en.prose:
The ancient storyteller begins by asking who first won great renown and placed a crown upon his head. The memory of that first king has faded from the ages, surviving only through what a son may hear from his father. The old chronicler tells how Kayumars established the throne and crown and became the first king. When the sun entered Aries, the world was renewed in glory, order, and water.

Kayumars made his first dwelling in the mountains. He and his companions wore leopard skins, and new forms of clothing and nourishment began with him. He ruled for thirty years and shone upon his throne like the sun. Beasts and creatures came from across the world to him, found peace under his protection, and learned the order of life from him.

His beloved son Siyamak was handsome, gifted, and ambitious. Kayumars cherished him deeply. Yet the evil Ahriman grew jealous and sent his mighty son, supported by a great army, against Siyamak in pursuit of the royal throne. The blessed Soroush warned Kayumars of the danger.

Siyamak gathered his forces and went to meet the demon. Since there was neither armor nor an established art of war, he covered himself with leopard skin. He fought Ahriman’s son bare-bodied, but the black demon struck him down with his claws and tore open his waist. Siyamak was killed, leaving the royal host without its leader.

Kayumars was overcome by grief. He descended from his throne in mourning, and the army, beasts, birds, and game joined the lament. For a full year they mourned Siyamak until Soroush brought a divine message: Kayumars must regain his composure, raise an army, cleanse the earth of the evil demon, and free his heart from grief.

Kayumars lifted his head toward heaven, invoked the highest name of God, wiped away his tears, and set out to avenge Siyamak. From then on he knew neither rest nor sleep, day or night.

zh.title: 凯尤马尔斯，第一位君王
zh.prose:
古老的史官开篇问道：世上第一个获得伟大声名、戴上王冠的人是谁？关于那位最初的君王，岁月已经几乎抹去了记忆，只有从父亲那里听来故事的儿子，才能将往事一一讲述。古老的记载说，凯尤马尔斯建立了王座与王冠的礼制，成为第一位君王。当太阳进入白羊座时，世界因荣耀、秩序与水而焕然一新。

凯尤马尔斯把最初的居所建在山中。他和同伴穿着豹皮，新的衣着与食物也从他的时代开始。他统治大地三十年，如太阳般在王座上闪耀。各种野兽与生灵从四面八方来到他身边，在他的庇护下获得安宁，并从他那里学习生活的秩序。

他的儿子西亚马克容貌俊美、才华出众而又追求声名，深受凯尤马尔斯爱护。然而邪恶的阿赫里曼心生嫉妒，派遣自己强大的儿子率领大军，企图夺取王座。吉祥的苏鲁什降临，向凯尤马尔斯警告了这场阴谋。

西亚马克召集军队迎战。那时还没有铠甲，也没有成熟的战争礼法，因此他用豹皮护身。他赤身与阿赫里曼之子搏斗，却被黑色魔鬼以利爪击倒并撕裂腰部。西亚马克战死，王族军队失去了领袖。

凯尤马尔斯悲痛欲绝，从王座上走下哀悼；军队、野兽、飞禽和猎兽也一同悲鸣。他们整整哀悼了一年，直到苏鲁什传来神圣的讯息：凯尤马尔斯必须恢复清醒，召集军队，清除大地上的恶魔，让心灵从悲痛中挣脱出来。

凯尤马尔斯抬头望天，呼唤至高的神名，擦去眼泪，踏上为西亚马克复仇的道路。从此，他日夜不息，再没有得到安宁与睡眠。

ar.title: كيومرث، أول الملوك
ar.prose:
يبدأ الراوي القديم بسؤال: من كان أول من نال العظمة في العالم ووضع التاج على رأسه؟ لقد طواها النسيان، ولم يبق من خبر ذلك الملك إلا ما يحفظه ابن عن أبيه. وتروي الأخبار القديمة أن كيومرث أسس العرش والتاج وكان أول ملك. وحين دخلت الشمس برج الحمل تجدد العالم بالمجد والنظام والماء.

اتخذ كيومرث مقامه الأول في الجبل، ولبس هو وأصحابه جلود النمور، وبدأ في عهده لباس وطعام جديدان. حكم ثلاثين عاماً، وكان يضيء على عرشه كالشمس. وأقبلت إليه الوحوش والمخلوقات من أنحاء العالم، فوجدت السكينة في جواره وتعلمت منه نظام الحياة.

كان له ابن محبوب اسمه سيامك، حسن الصورة موهوباً وطامحاً إلى المجد. أحبّه كيومرث حباً شديداً. لكن أهرمن الشرير حسده، وأرسل ابنه القوي بجيش كبير طمعاً في العرش والتاج. ونزل سروش المبارك ليحذر كيومرث من الخطر.

جمع سيامك جيشه وخرج لملاقاة العدو. ولم يكن يومها درع ولا نظام معروف للحرب، فغطى جسده بجلد النمر. اشتبك عارياً مع ابن أهرمن، لكن الشيطان الأسود ضربه بمخالبه وفتق خاصرته، فقُتل سيامك وبقي الجمع من غير قائد.

غلب الحزن كيومرث، فنزل عن عرشه نائحاً، وشارك الجيش والوحوش والطيور والصيد في الحداد. وظلوا عاماً كاملاً في حزنهم، حتى جاء سروش برسالة إلهية تأمر كيومرث أن يستعيد وعيه، ويجمع جيشاً، ويطهر الأرض من الشيطان، ويحرر قلبه من الحزن.

رفع كيومرث رأسه إلى السماء، ودعا باسم الإله الأعلى، ومسح دموعه، ثم اندفع للثأر لسيامك. ومنذ ذلك اليوم لم يعرف راحة ولا نوماً، ليلاً ولا نهاراً.

2.title: Part 2: Houshang, Founder of Civilization and Fire
2.prose:
After Kayumars, Houshang ascended the throne in his grandfather’s place. In the Shahnameh, he is a just and civilizing king: a ruler who does not seek kingship for power alone, but strives to bring order to human life and to open new ways of living.

At the beginning of his reign, the Shahnameh recalls among Houshang’s great achievements the discovery and use of iron for making tools. Blacksmithing and tools such as axes, saws, and adzes made human work easier, while irrigation and agriculture flourished. Houshang is presented as the figure who leads the world from a primitive way of life toward cultivation, craft, and ordered labor.

Yet the most celebrated episode of his reign is the discovery of fire. One day Houshang went toward the mountains with several companions. On the way, a black and terrifying serpent appeared. Houshang picked up a stone and hurled it at the serpent. The serpent escaped, and the stone struck another rock. From the meeting of the two stones came a brilliant spark, and fire was revealed.

The serpent was not killed, but Houshang understood the secret of this new radiance. He discovered that fire could be brought forth from the striking of stones: a gift that breaks the darkness, gives warmth, and would later become fundamental to cooking, craft, and human life.

Houshang did not claim the discovery as his own power. He prayed before the Creator and regarded the fire as a divine radiance. That night a great fire was kindled, and the people gathered around it. The celebration became known in the Shahnameh as Sadeh and remained as Houshang’s enduring memorial.

Houshang’s reign therefore marks a decisive stage in the progress of humanity: from understanding iron and making tools, to cultivating the land and discovering fire. That is why Ferdowsi closes this episode by remembering Houshang as the king who made the world more habitable and left behind a name honored for goodness.

3.title: Part 3: Tahmuras, Binder of Demons
3.prose:
After Houshang, Tahmuras came to the throne. In the Shahnameh, he is a brave and resourceful king who turns to battle in order to tame disorder and diminish the power of evil.

He is called “Binder of Demons” because he marched against the demons with great force and defeated them. In Ferdowsi’s telling, the demons and forces of Ahriman stand against the king, and Tahmuras overcomes them through a union of courage and wisdom.

At the beginning of his reign, Tahmuras works to cultivate and order the world, seeking to tame rebellious forces through strategy as well as strength. At last he resolves to march against the demons with his army. A fierce battle follows. Tahmuras prevails and takes many of them captive.

After their defeat, the demons offer Tahmuras a new form of knowledge in exchange for their freedom. They promise that, if the king releases them, they will teach him writing and the knowledge of script. Tahmuras accepts, and the Shahnameh thus establishes a striking bond between victory over the forces of chaos and the acquisition of knowledge.

After this victory, Tahmuras gains lasting renown, and the people remember his justice and strength. His story is one of the Shahnameh’s earliest images of human progress: after fire and tools in the age of Houshang, humanity now reaches writing and the preservation of knowledge.

The reign of Tahmuras ultimately opens the way for Jamshid, the king who will carry this movement into a far greater age of splendor, craft, and civilization.

4.title: Part 4: Jamshid, Glory and Fall
4.prose:
After Tahmuras, Jamshid ascended the throne, a king whose name in the Shahnameh is bound to the greatest age of flourishing and prosperity. At the beginning of his reign, he brought order to the world and expanded knowledge and craft.

Jamshid introduced many tools and new ways of living. He used iron to make weapons and useful implements, and organized the making of armor, clothing, and other human crafts. In his time, people were divided into different orders, each with a defined role, from priests and warriors to farmers and artisans.

Jamshid then turned to the ordering of everyday life. Building houses, providing clothing, advancing medicine, and discovering perfumes and precious stones are among the achievements attributed to him in the Shahnameh. He also expanded seafaring and means of transport, giving the world of the tale an unmistakable sense of civilization and splendor.

During this period, Jamshid fashioned a wondrous throne carried by demons, bearing the king from place to place. His glory rose so high that people came to regard his era as a golden age.

Jamshid later held a great festival and named it Nowruz. In it, people celebrated their release from hardship and remembered both their king and the prosperity of the world.

But the turning point comes when Jamshid exceeds the measure of his own place. Pride takes hold of him, and the divine glory, the farrah, withdraws. Once the king begins to see himself as the source of all splendor and power, his bond with justice and humility is broken.

The people turn away from him, and the way is opened for Zahhak. Jamshid, who once made the world prosperous, is driven into exile and remains hidden for years. At last Zahhak finds him and brings his life to an end.

Jamshid’s story in the Shahnameh holds two opposing faces: first, a human being who raises knowledge and civilization to their height; then a ruler consumed by self-regard, who loses what he himself had built.

5.title: Part 5: Zahhak, the Dragon’s Rise
5.prose:
After Jamshid’s fall, Iran entered a time of disorder, and the people longed for a powerful ruler. At that time Zahhak, the son of Mardas, lived in the land of the Arabs. He was a strong young man, but he also carried within him a powerful desire for authority and kingship.

Ahriman came to Zahhak in another guise and, through persuasive deceit, urged him to kill his father. Zahhak murdered Mardas by trickery and took power for himself. Ahriman then returned, this time presenting himself as a cook.

He prepared various dishes for Zahhak and won the young ruler’s trust. At last, seeking to please the king, he kissed his shoulders and suddenly disappeared. From the places of the kisses grew two black serpents, restless creatures that demanded human brains for food.

The physicians could do nothing to cure the affliction. Ahriman appeared again, now in the guise of a physician, and declared that the serpents could be quieted only by feeding them the brains of two young men each day. Thus Zahhak’s reign of terror and oppression began, placing the lives of countless youths in danger.

Meanwhile Jamshid, who had remained hidden after his defeat and exile, was finally captured by Zahhak. Zahhak killed him and claimed the throne. Under his rule, the people of Iran were subjected to fear and oppression.

To secure his power, Zahhak built a great palace and summoned priests and nobles. He wanted their confirmation that throughout his reign he had done nothing but justice and good. Yet his tyranny was so plain that even this outward approval revealed the fear under which the people lived.

Against this darkness, the story of Fereydun was taking shape. Fereydun was raised by his mother, Franak, far from Zahhak’s sight. In time, strengthened by the people and aided by Kaveh the Blacksmith, he rose against Zahhak.

Kaveh, who had lost sons and many young people to Zahhak’s cruelty, raised his blacksmith’s apron upon a spear and made it the banner of the uprising. The people gathered around Kaveh and Fereydun and rose to end Zahhak’s rule.

Fereydun marched to Zahhak’s palace, defeated him, and by the command of justice had him bound in Mount Damavand. The age of terror was brought to an end, and the way was opened for Fereydun’s reign.

Zahhak’s story is one of the Shahnameh’s clearest images of power that begins in deception, continues through bloodshed, and finally collapses before the will of the people and the force of justice.

6.title: Part 6: Fereydun and His Three Sons
6.prose: After defeating Zahhak and binding him in Damavand, Fereydun became king. His reign began in justice and peace, and the people recovered from years of oppression. He had three sons, whom he tested in disguise before dividing the world among them: Salm received the West, Tur the East, and Iraj, the youngest and dearest, received Iran. Salm and Tur grew jealous of Iraj’s share. Unlike them, Iraj valued peace above power and was even willing to surrender his claim to prevent bloodshed. They mistook his generosity for weakness, murdered him, and sent his severed head to Fereydun. The old king was plunged into grief, and the murder became the beginning of a blood-feud that would shape generations. Fereydun placed his hope in Iraj’s descendants and raised Manuchehr to avenge his grandfather. What began as a division meant to establish order thus became the source of a hatred that would endure for generations.

7.title: Part 7: Iraj and the Vengeance
7.prose: After Iraj’s murder, Fereydun’s peaceful hope gave way to grief and the memory of blood. From Iraj’s line came Manuchehr, whom Fereydun raised for kingship and for the recovery of Iraj’s right. When Manuchehr reached manhood, he marched toward Turan with renowned champions. Tur, one of the chief authors of Iraj’s death, met him in battle and was killed. Salm survived longer, but Manuchehr defeated him as well. The heads of both brothers were brought before Fereydun, who felt sorrow mingled with a measure of peace: Iraj’s blood had finally been answered by his own descendants. Yet the tale also reveals the cost of vengeance. Manuchehr sought to restore a broken order, but one crime had already created a feud capable of crossing generations. His victories prepared the way for him to succeed Fereydun and opened the heroic age that would follow.

8.title: Part 8: Manuchehr and the Dawn of the Heroic Age
8.prose: After Manuchehr avenged Iraj, Fereydun named him his successor. Manuchehr took the throne bearing the legacy and sacred glory of Iraj’s house. In his final years, Fereydun urged him to rule with justice and guard Iran’s borders, knowing that the feud with Tur’s descendants had not ended. Renowned champions gathered around the new king, including Qaren, while the house of Sam rose to prominence. Across the frontier, Pashang and the descendants of Tur prepared to oppose Iran, and the old hostility became the source of future wars between Iran and Turan. Manuchehr was not merely heir to the throne; he saw himself as heir to Iraj’s blood and ancestral legacy. His reign therefore forms a bridge between the first kings and the heroic age. As it draws to a close, Sam moves toward the center of the story, and the tale of Zal begins.

9.title: Part 9: Sam and Zal
9.part: Zal and the House of Sam
9.prose:
In the reign of Manuchehr, Sam Nariman was the greatest champion of Iran and stood high in the king’s esteem. Sam had a son whose appearance at birth set him apart from other children: the child’s hair was white, and this filled his father with unease.

Fearing the judgment of others, Sam believed the child unworthy of his name and ordered that the infant be carried to Mount Alborz and abandoned there. The helpless child was found by the Simurgh, who carried him to her nest. She raised him among her own young, and the child grew beneath the mountain skies beside the legendary bird.

Years later, Sam learned of his son in a dream. Regret overcame him, and he journeyed to Alborz. There he saw the Simurgh and discovered that the child was alive. The bird made him understand that a child’s appearance should never have been a reason for rejection.

Sam repented and begged the Simurgh to return his son. She gave the child back and, before they parted, gave Sam a feather from her wing. She told him that if a grave danger ever came, he should cast the feather into the fire, and she would come to his aid.

Sam took the child back to Zabulistan and named him Zal. Zal grew beside his father, and in time his wisdom and courage became unmistakable. His return to the house of Sam opened an important new chapter in Iran’s heroic tradition; one day he would be joined to Rudabeh, and from their union Rustam, the greatest champion of the Shahnameh, would be born.

10.title: Part 10: Zal and the Simurgh
10.part: Zal and the House of Sam
10.prose:
After returning to Zabulistan, Zal grew under Sam’s care, gaining knowledge and strength year by year. Yet his bond with the Simurgh never disappeared. She had not merely raised him in childhood; she had become part of the course of his destiny.

In youth, Zal became a champion distinguished by wisdom as much as by strength. He did not rely on his arm alone. In difficult decisions he also relied on reflection and foresight, qualities that would set him apart from many other heroes.

During one of the great trials of his life, Sam called upon him for help in a difficult campaign. Zal encountered dangers along the way and understood that human strength is not always enough. At that moment, the memory of the Simurgh returned to him.

Zal cast into the fire the feather she had given him in childhood. Soon the Simurgh appeared, ready to aid him. Her return showed that their bond belonged not only to his childhood, but also to the moments when his destiny was being decided.

The Simurgh showed Zal the way forward and delivered him from danger. Zal learned that courage becomes greater when joined with wisdom, experience, and the right counsel, and that even the hardest road may be crossed by one who knows when to seek guidance.

She also warned him against haste and pride. Strength without wisdom, she taught him, can lead to ruin; a champion must recognize the right path before drawing the sword.

The bond between Zal and the Simurgh is one of the Shahnameh’s most distinctive relationships. To Zal, she is at once a foster mother, a teacher, and a mysterious helper who appears at decisive moments.

Her importance will grow in the years ahead. When Zal meets Rudabeh and their love becomes a crisis between two houses, the Simurgh will again touch the fate of his family. Even at Rustam’s birth, her knowledge and aid will prove lifesaving.

Thus the story of Zal and the Simurgh is more than the tale of an abandoned child and a legendary bird. It is the making of Zal’s heroic identity—and of a bond whose consequences will reach into the next generation and shape the destiny of Iran’s greatest hero.

11.title: Part 11: Zal and Rudabeh
11.part: Zal and the House of Sam
11.prose:
After returning to Zabulistan, Sam’s son Zal became a renowned champion, admired for both courage and wisdom. His fame crossed the borders of Iran and reached distant lands. In those years, fate brought him together with Rudabeh, daughter of Mehrab Shah of Kabul.

Rudabeh was beautiful, intelligent, and brave. Mehrab belonged to the house of Zahhak, and that lineage placed a formidable obstacle before the marriage from the very beginning. Sam and the elders of Iran could not easily consent to such a union.

At their first meeting, Zal fell in love with Rudabeh, and she with him. Yet their love could not proceed openly or without danger. Rudabeh found a secret way to meet him and lowered her long hair from the palace so that Zal could climb to her.

They pledged themselves to one another, knowing that their families would be difficult to persuade. When Mehrab learned of their love, he was furious. In Iran, Sam likewise objected, troubled by the history of Rudabeh’s lineage.

Zal refused to abandon his love. He believed a person should be judged by character and wisdom, not by ancestry alone. His resolve became a test of maturity: he had to find a path between the desire of his heart and his duties to his family and country.

He therefore appealed to the elders and to King Manuchehr, arguing that Rudabeh was worthy of him and that their marriage could turn inherited hostility into a new bond between houses.

Manuchehr consulted astrologers and priests. They examined the signs of the stars and foretold that a child of Zal and Rudabeh would be born—a peerless champion whose name would resound throughout the world.

After the prophecy, opposition softened. Sam finally gave his consent, and Mehrab agreed to his daughter’s marriage. Zal and Rudabeh were wed with celebration and splendor, joining the two houses.

Their marriage is one of the great turning points of the Shahnameh, for from it Rustam will be born. Their love is therefore more than a romance: it is the meeting point of the house of Sam, the royal lineage, and the destiny of Iran’s greatest champion.

12.title: Part 12: The Birth of Rustam
12.prose:
After Zal and Rudabeh were married, a new chapter began in their lives. In time Rudabeh became pregnant, but as the hour of childbirth approached, her pain grew so severe that everyone understood this would not be an ordinary birth.

Rudabeh writhed in agony, while Zal was helpless. None of the usual means seemed enough to save mother and child. Zal remembered the Simurgh, the bird who had been his companion and guide since childhood.

He cast into the fire the Simurgh feather he had kept all those years. Soon the Simurgh appeared and told him that Rudabeh could be saved only through a difficult but necessary procedure. At her command, a wise and skilled physician was summoned to deliver the child by opening Rudabeh’s side.

Rudabeh was rendered unconscious, and an incision was made in her side. The child was brought out, and the wound was treated and closed with medicine. Mother and child both survived the great danger.

The child was strong and broad-built, bearing from the beginning signs of an extraordinary destiny. Zal named him Rustam—a name that would one day become inseparable from heroism, strength, and loyalty throughout Iran and beyond.

Once the Simurgh was assured that mother and child were safe, she returned to her mountain abode. Her feather, however, remained with Zal’s family, so that she might be summoned again should grave danger arise.

From childhood, Rustam was unlike other children. He grew rapidly, and his physical strength and intelligence soon became evident. Zal understood that this child was not destined for an ordinary life, and that his fate would be bound to the fate of Iran.

Rustam’s birth in the Shahnameh is more than the birth of a champion: it marks the beginning of the age of Rustam, when many of Iran’s greatest heroic tales will unfold. From battles with demons and dragons to the Seven Labors, the wars between Iran and Turan, and the tragic tale of Rustam and Sohrab, his name will stand at the center of the story.

Thus the union of Zal and Rudabeh brought forth a child who carried the inheritance of three worlds within him: the wisdom and royal glory of Sam’s house, Rudabeh’s love and nobility, and the wondrous aid of the Simurgh.

13.title: Part 13: Rustam and Rakhsh
13.prose:
From childhood, Rustam possessed a strength beyond that of others, and it soon became clear that he was destined to become a great champion. As the years passed, the time came for him to find a worthy horse—one strong enough to accompany him on journeys and in war.

Rustam tested many horses, but none could bear his weight and power. At last he heard of a herd in the land of Zabul. Among them was a powerful, swift young horse that had never been tamed.

Rustam saw that this horse was unlike the others. Its coat was dark reddish, and for this reason it was named Rakhsh. It possessed not only immense strength but also extraordinary intelligence and courage.

Rustam wanted to take Rakhsh with him, but the keeper of the herd resisted, fearing the horses’ owner. Rustam made it clear through both his words and his strength that this was the horse meant for him. At last he won Rakhsh, and from that day the two were inseparable.

A bond grew between them that was more than that of rider and horse. Rakhsh often sensed danger before Rustam did and sometimes acted without waiting for his master’s command. Rustam, in turn, trusted him completely.

On their journeys, Rakhsh bore the champion’s weight and heavy saddle; in battle he charged without fear. Together they crossed plains, deserts, and enemy lands, and Rakhsh shared in many of Rustam’s victories.

Above all, Rakhsh was loyal. When Rustam slept or was unaware, Rakhsh guarded him and stood against beasts and enemies. In this way, the horse became part of Rustam’s heroic identity.

In the Shahnameh, Rustam is almost unimaginable without Rakhsh. Together they form an epic pair: a champion of extraordinary human strength and a horse endowed with legendary intelligence and power.

From this point onward, wherever Rustam undertakes a great journey or enters a great battle, Rakhsh will be beside him. Their bond will reveal its strength again and again, from the Seven Labors to the wars between Iran and Turan.

14.title: Part 14: Rustam’s Seven Labors
14.prose:
By the time Rustam had become one of Iran’s greatest champions, he was entrusted with a perilous mission. King Kay Kavus had led the Iranian army into Mazandaran, where, through treachery and sorcery, he was captured and blinded along with his soldiers.

Rustam set out for Mazandaran to rescue the king and the Iranian host. The road before him passed through seven perilous stages, each testing his strength, judgment, and will in a different way. He crossed them with Rakhsh, and the journey became known as the Seven Labors.

In the first labor, Rustam encountered a mighty lion. Before Rustam could awaken, Rakhsh fought the beast and killed it. When Rustam awoke, he understood that his horse had saved his life.

In the second labor, Rustam crossed a dry, scorching desert. Thirst brought both him and Rakhsh close to exhaustion. Searching desperately for water, Rustam finally found a spring by following a sign in the wilderness and escaped death.

In the third labor, a terrible dragon barred their way. It concealed itself, revealing its presence only for brief moments. Rakhsh sensed the danger and woke Rustam. Together they fought and finally slew the dragon.

In the fourth labor, a sorceress appeared before Rustam in the guise of a beautiful and benevolent woman. Rustam asked her to speak the name of God. Unable to conceal her true nature, she was revealed in her real form, and Rustam destroyed her.

In the fifth labor, Rustam encountered Olad, a champion of Mazandaran. After defeating him, Rustam promised to spare and reward him if he showed the way through Mazandaran and led him to the White Demon. Olad agreed and became his guide.

In the sixth labor, Rustam fought Arzhang Div. He entered the midst of the demons and killed Arzhang, clearing the way toward the White Demon.

In the seventh labor, Rustam reached the cave of the White Demon, one of the mightiest demons of Mazandaran. His sorcery had caused Kay Kavus and the Iranian army to lose their sight. After a fierce struggle, Rustam defeated and killed him.

Rustam used the White Demon’s blood to restore the sight of Kay Kavus and his soldiers. Once their vision returned, the king and the Iranian host were freed, and Rustam had once again saved Iran from a great danger.

The Seven Labors are more than a sequence of battles. At each stage Rustam confronts a different form of danger: animal force, thirst, the unknown monster, deception, a human adversary, and finally demonic power. His victories come from the union of strength, vigilance, Rakhsh’s loyalty, and endurance in the face of hardship.

15.title: Part 15: Rustam and Sohrab
15.prose:
Years after Rustam’s youth, a horse accompanying him was lost in the land of Samangan. Rustam went there in search of Rakhsh. The king of Samangan welcomed him and promised to find the missing horse.

That night, Tahmineh, the king’s daughter, secretly came to Rustam. She had known his fame since childhood and had heard the stories of his courage. She asked him to take her as his wife. Rustam accepted, and from their union a son named Sohrab was born.

When Rustam departed, he gave Tahmineh an armband and told her to place it on their child if the child proved to be a boy. Sohrab grew swiftly into a powerful young warrior. Yet he did not know who his father was.

As a youth, Sohrab asked his mother about his father and learned that Rustam was the man who had sired him. From then on, he longed to find his father and stand beside him. But fate prepared another road.

Sohrab joined the army of Turan. Afrasiyab, aware of the young warrior’s strength, secretly devised a plan to keep father and son from recognizing one another and, if possible, to make each destroy the other.

Sohrab entered Iran with his army and captured fortresses along the way. Kay Kavus learned of the young warrior’s advance and sent Rustam to oppose him. The two champions faced one another on the battlefield without knowing their true relationship.

From their first encounter, Sohrab suspected that the strength of his opponent belonged to Rustam. Several times he asked whether the warrior before him was Rustam. Rustam concealed his identity and presented himself as an ordinary fighter. That concealment became the seed of tragedy.

The two champions fought more than once. In their first combat, Sohrab overcame Rustam, but Rustam survived through experience and deception. In the next encounter, Rustam threw Sohrab down and dealt him a mortal wound.

As he lay dying, Sohrab spoke of his name and lineage and showed the armband his mother had given him. When Rustam saw it, he realized that the young man he had struck down was his own son.

Rustam collapsed beneath grief and remorse. He called for physicians and sought Kay Kavus’s help, but it was too late. Sohrab died, and Rustam was left in profound mourning.

When Tahmineh heard of her son’s death, she was devastated. Rustam, too, carried the memory of Sohrab with him for the rest of his life.

The story of Rustam and Sohrab is one of the Shahnameh’s most painful tragedies: a father and son who were both seeking one another, brought face to face on a battlefield, yet separated before they could know the truth by concealment and deception.

16.title: Part 16: Siavash
16.prose:
Siavash, son of Kay Kavus and one of the Shahnameh’s purest and noblest figures, was raised from childhood under Rustam’s care. Rustam took him to Zabul and taught him the ways of knighthood, horsemanship, archery, and honor. Siavash grew into a thoughtful, calm, and courageous young man, and when he returned to court he won the admiration of all.

Sudabeh, the wife of Kay Kavus, became enamored of Siavash and tried to draw him toward her. Siavash refused her advances. After being rejected, however, Sudabeh presented the matter differently and accused him.

Kay Kavus was caught between his wife’s words and his trust in his son’s innocence. To prove his purity, Siavash agreed to pass through a great fire. A huge fire was prepared, and Siavash rode through the flames on his horse and emerged unharmed. The people took this as proof of his innocence, and the accusation fell away.

After this ordeal, Siavash no longer regarded the court as a safe place. When war with Turan began, Kay Kavus appointed him commander of the army. Siavash won victories in battle, but against the wishes of the court he chose reconciliation and an end to bloodshed.

Afrasiyab, king of Turan, also accepted Siavash’s proposal for peace. Siavash asked Kay Kavus to accept the agreement, but the king became angry and ordered the war to continue.

Unwilling to break the treaty or shed the blood of hostages, Siavash chose to leave Iran and go to Turan. Afrasiyab welcomed him at first and honored him. In Turan, Siavash married Farangis, Afrasiyab’s daughter, and began a new life.

Yet the suspicion and hostility of some Turanian courtiers, especially Garsivaz, eventually destroyed his peace. The story of Siavash now moves toward one of the Shahnameh’s darkest tragedies: the story of a man who stood between political power and moral conscience, and paid for his loyalty to his word and his own purity.

17.title: Part 17: Siavash in Turan
17.prose:
After entering Turan, Siavash was at first received with great honor. Afrasiyab, having learned of his wisdom and courage, welcomed him as a distinguished guest and granted him part of his land. There Siavash turned away from war and vengeance and devoted himself instead to building and cultivation.

He founded a city in Turan known as Siavashgerd and raised palaces and other great buildings beside it. His new life was also joined to Farangis, Afrasiyab’s daughter, and for a time he lived peacefully with his family.

But his peace did not last. Garsivaz, Afrasiyab’s brother, grew fearful of Siavash’s position and planted suspicion against him in the king’s mind. He fabricated reports that portrayed Siavash as a conspirator and traitor.

Afrasiyab, who had once honored Siavash, gradually fell under the influence of these suspicions. Siavash tried to defend himself, but the court was no longer a place where justice could be heard.

Farangis was deeply concerned for her husband’s life. Even knowing the danger, Siavash refused to save himself through deceit or civil conflict. He continued to hold to purity and self-restraint.

At last Afrasiyab ordered Siavash’s arrest. He was torn from the palace and the peaceful life he had built and led toward death. Even in his final moments, Siavash refused vengeance and accepted his fate with composure.

Siavash’s death in Turan was not merely the end of a prince’s life. It left a wound between Iran and Turan. His blood would later become the source of great acts of vengeance, and his name would endure as a symbol of innocence, injustice suffered, and faithfulness to one’s word.

18.title: Part 18: The Death of Siavash
18.prose:
Siavash became trapped in the suspicion and intrigue of Afrasiab’s court in Turan. Garsivaz, who feared his influence and popularity, filled Afrasiab’s mind with false accusations until suspicion hardened into a sentence of death.

Siavash knew there was no escape. Farangis, his wife and Afrasiab’s daughter, tried to save him, but the king’s command remained. Even in his final moments, Siavash spoke neither of hatred nor revenge; he met his fate with composure.

He was taken from the court and delivered to Garsivaz and Afrasiab’s men. At last, by Afrasiab’s order, Siavash was killed. His blood fell upon the earth, but his death was not the end of his story.

After Siavash’s death, Farangis was left in mourning. Their son, Kay Khusrow, was still alive. Pirân Visah, one of the wisest nobles of Turan, worked to protect Farangis and the child and keep them beyond the reach of danger.

When news of Siavash’s death reached Iran, the people were stricken with grief. Rustam, who had raised Siavash almost as his own son, was consumed by anger and marched toward Turan to avenge his blood.

The vengeance for Siavash did not remain a private feud. His blood became a sign of injustice and drew later generations into a long confrontation with Turan. In time, Kay Khusrow, Siavash’s son, returned to Iran, and much of his life and reign became bound to the demand for justice for his father.

The death of Siavash is one of the Shahnameh’s central tragedies: a pure hero killed not because he was defeated in battle, but because of suspicion, conspiracy, and injustice—and that injustice set in motion a long cycle of vengeance.

19.title: Part 19: Kay Khusrow
19.prose:
After Siavash’s death, Farangis and her son Kay Khusrow remained in Turan. Kay Khusrow grew up under the protection of Pirân Visah, a wise man who stood apart from the intrigues of Afrasiab’s court and sought to keep the boy alive.

At last Rustam and the nobles of Iran learned that Siavash’s son was still alive. Gudarz received signs of Kay Khusrow in a dream and sent his son Giv to Turan to find him. After a long search, Giv found Farangis and Kay Khusrow and brought them toward Iran.

Their return was dangerous. Afrasiab learned that they had fled and sent an army after them, but Giv and his companions succeeded in crossing out of Turan and reaching Iran.

Kay Kavus, seeing his grandson, judged Kay Khusrow worthy of the throne. Yet his accession was preceded by rivalry among nobles and claimants. In the end, with the support of the great men of Iran and the signs of his lineage and worth, Kay Khusrow became king.

From the beginning, unlike many earlier kings, Kay Khusrow did not seek kingship merely for splendor or power. His chief purpose was to avenge Siavash and restore justice. He organized the Iranian forces and prepared great champions such as Rustam, Gudarz, Giv, and Tus for war against Turan.

The great wars between Iran and Turan intensified during his reign. Through successive battles, Kay Khusrow finally defeated Afrasiab and, after years of pursuit, obtained vengeance for his father’s blood.

Yet at the end of his path, Kay Khusrow, like several of the Shahnameh’s great kings, turned away from worldly power. Before his departure he named a successor and withdrew from the throne. He then went into the mountains and disappeared, a departure that the Shahnameh surrounds with an atmosphere of sanctity and mystery.

Kay Khusrow carries the story of Siavash from tragedy toward justice: a king who fulfilled his father’s legacy and, in the end, turned away from kingship and the material world itself.

20.title: Part 20: Rustam and Esfandiyar
20.prose:
Esfandiyar, son of Goshtasp, was a renowned champion and a formidable warrior. He was deeply loyal to the king and had repeatedly gone to battle for the Iranian throne. Yet Goshtasp, seeking to keep his son at a distance, placed one difficult mission after another upon him.

On one such mission Esfandiyar went to Turan, defeated the enemy, and freed his sisters, Homay and Beh-Afarid, from the captivity of Arjasp. When he returned, he expected Goshtasp to honor his promise, but the king imposed another heavy command: he was to bring Rustam to court in chains.

Rustam, the aged and greatest of Iran’s champions, was willing to go before the king, but he would not enter the court like a captive. Esfandiyar, for his part, regarded Goshtasp’s command as an obligation. Their conversation reached an impasse, and at last battle became unavoidable.

The two champions fought several times. Because of his extraordinary armor and strength, Esfandiyar was protected from ordinary blows. Rustam was wounded and, seeking help, remembered the Simurgh.

The Simurgh healed Rustam and showed him how Esfandiyar could be defeated. In the next battle, Rustam used a special bow and an arrow made from the wood of the گز tree, aiming at Esfandiyar’s eye and dealing him a mortal wound.

In his final moments Esfandiyar understood that death was near. He reproached Rustam, yet he also knew that he had become the victim of Goshtasp’s command. Then he entrusted his son Bahman to Rustam, asking him to teach the boy the code of the champions.

Rustam grieved for Esfandiyar, for he had never wished to stain his hands with the blood of such a hero. Their battle was not a simple victory of one champion over another, but the tragedy of two great men caught between duty, the king’s command, and fate.

The story of Rustam and Esfandiyar shows that in the Shahnameh even heroism and loyalty can become catastrophic when joined to a misguided command and the hunger for power.

21.title: Part 21: Rustam and Shaghad
21.prose:
Shaghad was Rustam’s half-brother. Though he belonged to the lineage of heroes, he carried resentment toward Rustam and secretly joined the King of Kabul in a plot to destroy him.

Shaghad pretended to Zal and Rustam that he had fallen into conflict with the King of Kabul. Rustam went to Kabul to support his brother, unaware that Shaghad had secretly made an agreement with the king.

The King of Kabul prepared a great pit in Rustam’s path and filled it with spears and blades, then concealed it beneath branches and earth. As Rustam traveled with Rakhsh and several companions, the ground suddenly gave way. Horse and rider fell into the pit; Rakhsh was pierced by the spears and Rustam was terribly wounded.

Rustam understood that this was no accident. Seeing Shaghad, he realized that his brother had taken part in the betrayal. Even with mortal wounds, he still had the strength to act. He asked Shaghad for his bow and arrows, then told him to hide behind a tree.

With his last strength Rustam released an arrow. It passed through the tree and pinned Shaghad to its trunk. Thus Rustam answered his brother’s treachery, though he himself could no longer survive.

Before dying, Rustam remembered Rakhsh and the years of his heroic life and bade farewell to the world. With his death, Zal and the heroic house lost one of the greatest pillars of Iran’s epic tradition.

The death of Rustam marks the end of a great age of heroism in the Shahnameh. He did not fall before a mighty enemy on the battlefield, but through the hidden treachery of those closest to him.

22.title: Part 22: After Rustam — The Legacy of the Heroes
22.prose:
After the deaths of Rustam and Shaghad, the heroic world of Iran was no longer what it had been. Rustam’s death was not merely the loss of a champion; it marked the end of an age in which the fate of Iran was bound above all to the names of its great heroes.

Zal, Rustam’s father, was devastated. The house of Sam and Zal, for generations a pillar of Iranian heroism, now faced the absence left by its greatest champion. Yet Rustam’s name and legacy remained alive among heroes and people.

Other champions sought to defend Iran after Rustam. Farāmarz, his son, became one of the most important figures of this generation, following his father’s path and earning renown in many battles.

Yet this was an age of change. Kings and armies continued to fight Iran’s enemies, but no single champion could again occupy the place Rustam held in the imagination of the people.

Heroic tales increasingly moved from one central champion to a company of heroes. Farāmarz, Giv, Gudarz, Tus, and others each carried part of the previous generation’s legacy.

Rustam’s death showed that even the greatest champion is not beyond fate or betrayal. He was not defeated by an enemy’s strength; deceit among those close to him prepared the way for his death.

From this point, Rustam’s memory remains alive while the story of Iran moves toward new generations and events. It is a passage between the age of renowned champions and the increasingly historical and political chapters of the epic.

Rustam’s legacy was more than victory: loyalty, defense of Iran, kinship with the people, and resistance to oppression continued in the stories of those who followed.

23.title: Part 23: Farāmarz and the Legacy of Rustam
23.prose:
After the grief over Rustam’s death began to recede, his name and family remained woven into the history of Iran. Farāmarz, Rustam’s son, carried his father’s legacy. Trained in warfare, horsemanship, and courage, he sought to keep alive the name of the house of Sam and Zal.

Farāmarz lived in an age when Iran needed new champions. Hostility with Turan continued, and the Iranian court depended on the strength and experience of its heroes to defend its borders.

In the battles that followed Rustam, Farāmarz fought beside the other Iranian champions. His name appears in the accounts of wars with Turan and the great campaigns of this period. Yet his own fate, like that of many heroes of Rustam’s house, was tragic.

In one great confrontation, Farāmarz was captured by the enemy. Despite defeat and captivity, he did not abandon the code and honor of a champion. His enemies eventually killed him, and the news reached Iran.

His death showed that with Rustam gone, suffering and danger had not left his family. One generation of heroes after another was lost in war, and Iran paid a heavy price to preserve its independence.

Yet the legacy of this house was not contained in the deaths of its champions. Each generation passed part of its experience, name, and culture of heroism to the next. Thus, even after Rustam and Farāmarz were gone, their stories remained alive in Iran’s memory.

This was a time of transition: Rustam’s glory still overshadowed everything, but the Shahnameh gradually turned toward other heroes and rulers, expanding from the story of one central champion into a wider constellation of lives and destinies.

24.title: Part 24: Gudarz and Giv — Pillars of the Iranian Army
24.prose:
After the age of Rustam and Farāmarz, the heroes of Iran remained engaged in great wars with Turan. In this period, the name of Gudarz and his family became increasingly prominent. Gudarz, the veteran elder of the Iranian army, had fought beside kings and champions for many years and possessed deep experience of both the battlefield and politics.

Gudarz’s family was not limited to him. His son Giv was also one of Iran’s great champions and played a role in many of the Shahnameh’s most important events. The bond between father and son was an example of the transmission of experience and the code of chivalry from one generation to another.

On the battlefield, Gudarz did not rely on strength alone. Again and again, through foresight and an understanding of the enemy, he guided the Iranian army through great dangers. Giv too was a courageous young hero, and in difficult missions—especially the search for Kay Khusrow—he proved his worth.

In the time of Kay Khusrow, Gudarz’s family became one of the main pillars of the Iranian army. Gudarz’s sons and descendants took part in many battles, and many of them gave their lives defending Iran.

Opposing this family, the army of Turan also had great heroic houses. The conflict between Iran and Turan was therefore no longer merely a confrontation between two kings; entire families of champions and successive generations were drawn into it.

This period shows that after Rustam’s death, the burden of the epic fell upon a group of heroes. Gudarz, Giv, and their family filled part of the great absence left behind and expanded the story of Iran from that of a single hero into a network of heroic families.

The names of Gudarz and Giv also remind us that in the Shahnameh, heroism does not depend on individual strength alone. Experience, family loyalty, strategic wisdom, and responsibility toward the homeland are all part of what it means to be a champion.

25.title: Part 25: Kay Khusrow’s Vengeance and the Great War
25.prose:
After Kay Khusrow returned to Iran, one of the greatest confrontations between Iran and Turan began. Holding Afrasiab responsible for Siavash’s blood, Kay Khusrow resolved to bring justice for his father to its conclusion. He gathered the Iranian army and entrusted command of its different divisions to renowned champions.

In this campaign, Gudarz, Giv, Tus, Fariburz, and other heroes each led a part of the army. Rustam remained the greatest support of Iran’s military power. On the other side, Afrasiab also assembled a great army from Turan.

Battles took place across different lands. At times the Iranian army prevailed, and at other times the Turanians gained the upper hand. But Kay Khusrow’s goal was not simply victory in a single field. He wanted to break the power that had threatened Iran for so many years.

In one of the most important stages of the war, the Iranian champions faced the Turanian army, and many renowned warriors on both sides were killed. These wars showed how the blood of Siavash had become a broad hostility between two lands.

Afrasiab repeatedly tried to escape Kay Khusrow. He moved from city to city and made use of different fortresses and places of refuge. But Kay Khusrow and the Iranian army continued their pursuit.

In the end, the Turanian army suffered a crushing defeat and Afrasiab was forced to flee. After years of waiting, Kay Khusrow had come close to his central purpose: finding the enemy who had caused his father’s death.

Yet the victory came at a heavy price. Many champions and soldiers died on the battlefields, and lands were repeatedly devastated. These wars are not merely the story of a victory; they tell of a generation that spent much of its life beneath the shadow of vengeance and war.

At last, Kay Khusrow succeeded in trapping Afrasiab and avenging the blood of Siavash. Yet Afrasiab’s end was not the complete end of hostility between Iran and Turan, for the wounds of years of war remained in the memory of both lands.

26.title: Part 26: Lohrasp and the End of Kay Khusrow’s Age
26.prose:
After Kay Khusrow brought his years of kingship, great wars, and vengeance for Siavash to an end, he gradually turned away from the world and the splendor of the throne. He was a king who had spent much of his life pursuing justice for his father, and now, having reached his goal, he thought more deeply about the impermanence of power.

Kay Khusrow finally decided to entrust the throne to a man who could continue ruling Iran after him. He judged Lohrasp, of the line of Kay Qobad, worthy of succession and handed the crown and throne to him. For many of the champions this was not easy to accept; they considered Rustam, Gudarz, Giv, and other great men worthy of kingship and were surprised that Kay Khusrow had chosen another man.

Nevertheless, Kay Khusrow stood by his decision and asked the champions to support the new order. Lohrasp accepted the kingship and took upon himself the heavy responsibility of guarding Iran. Thus one of the Shahnameh’s brightest heroic periods gradually gave way to a new era, in which the names of Goshtasp and then Esfandiyar would become more prominent.

After surrendering the throne, Kay Khusrow prepared to depart. He said farewell to his companions and champions and renounced the attachments of the world. Many of the great men wished to persuade him to change his decision, but Kay Khusrow had chosen his path. For him, remaining in power was no longer the goal; once his duty had been fulfilled, kingship had to be entrusted to another.

Kay Khusrow went toward the mountains with several companions. On the way, signs of danger appeared and the weather changed. Snow and a violent storm closed in, and the group became trapped among the mountains. Some companions could go no farther, but Kay Khusrow continued and finally disappeared from sight.

The end of Kay Khusrow’s life in the Shahnameh is unlike the deaths of many kings. He is not killed in battle, nor does an enemy destroy him; instead, he withdraws from the world and disappears into the mountains. This mysterious ending reflects the difference between his kingship and that of other rulers.

With Kay Khusrow’s departure, Lohrasp takes the throne and Iran enters a new stage. Kay Khusrow leaves more than a crown and throne behind: he leaves the memory of Siavash’s blood, victory over Afrasiab, and an example of renouncing power. From here the story moves toward Goshtasp, Zoroaster, and then the battles of Esfandiyar, beginning a new age of epic history.

27.title: Part 27: Goshtasp and the Coming of Zoroaster
27.prose:
After Kay Khusrow withdrew from the world and Lohrasp took the throne, the age of the Kayanids entered a new phase. Lohrasp began his reign, but among his sons and successors, Goshtasp became especially important to Iran’s future. Goshtasp was ambitious and strong, and because his future claim to the throne seemed uncertain, he came into conflict with his father.

The dispute eventually drove Goshtasp away from Iran. He traveled toward Rome and came to a land where he met Katayun, the daughter of the Roman Caesar. Contrary to the expectations of the court, Katayun chose Goshtasp, and their union prepared the way for his return to Iran and the strengthening of his position. After his return, Goshtasp once again entered the center of power, and his fate became bound to the future of the Iranian empire.

In this same period, a great event took place in Iran’s culture and religion: Zoroaster came to Goshtasp with a new message and faith. In the Shahnameh’s account, he called people to the path of truth, justice, purity, and avoidance of falsehood. Zoroaster’s coming was not merely a change in religious belief; within the epic story, it marked the beginning of an era in which Goshtasp’s kingship became bound to a new faith and its defense.

Goshtasp accepted this faith, and a number of nobles joined him. The new religion did not please everyone. Resistance arose at court and among opposing political forces, while the hostility of Arjasp, king of Turan, intensified. In his eyes, the change of faith in Iran was not merely a religious matter; it signaled a political and cultural transformation that could alter the balance between Iran and Turan.

To establish the new faith, Goshtasp needed the support of his family and champions. Zarir, his brother, became one of the first great defenders and warriors of this period. Soon Esfandiyar, Goshtasp’s son, also emerged as the most important military figure of the family—a champion who would play a decisive role both in defending Iran and in Goshtasp’s own fate.

Meanwhile, Arjasp was preparing to confront Iran. The acceptance of the new faith became a pretext for new wars, followed by threatening messages and Turanian campaigns. Thus religious transformation became linked to a major political and military confrontation, and Iran once again stood against Turan.

At this stage Goshtasp is more than the king of a country. He stands where the Kayanid royal tradition meets a new faith and a new generation of champions. From this point, Zarir and especially Esfandiyar move to the center of the story, and the struggle with Arjasp lays the groundwork for one of the Shahnameh’s great later tragedies. Goshtasp’s story is therefore a bridge between the age of Kay Khusrow and the world of Esfandiyar, a world in which religion, power, family, and war become increasingly intertwined.

28.title: Part 28: The War Between Iran and Turan and Arjasp
28.prose:
Goshtasp’s acceptance of Zoroaster’s faith was not merely a change within the Iranian court; in the world of the Shahnameh, it also provoked Iran’s enemies. Arjasp, king of Turan, grew angry at the spread of the new faith and condemned Goshtasp for the change. When he received Goshtasp’s reply, threats turned into a military campaign, and once again the borders of Iran and Turan stood on the brink of war.

Arjasp assembled a great army and marched toward Iran. His aim was not merely to defeat a king; he wanted to crush the new political and cultural force that had taken shape in Iran. The Turanian army approached Iranian lands, and cities and religious centers came under threat. Goshtasp was forced to prepare his army and defend both his country and the new faith.

Among the Iranians, Zarir, Goshtasp’s brother, was among the first to bear the burden of war. He was an experienced and loyal champion and led the Iranian army in battle. The opening clashes were fierce and bloody, and both sides suffered heavy losses. The war was no longer a simple confrontation between two kings; many families and champions were drawn into it, and Iran’s fate depended on their courage.

In one of the great battles, Zarir fought with extraordinary bravery, but was eventually killed. His death dealt a heavy blow to Goshtasp and the Iranian army. Yet the defeat and death of the champions did not completely destroy the Iranians’ strength and resolve. On the contrary, Zarir’s death became a sign of the high price of defending Iran and brought a new generation of warriors into the field.

In this period Esfandiyar rose ever more prominently. He was Goshtasp’s son and one of the strongest champions of his generation. Esfandiyar was loyal to the new faith and possessed great military ability. After the death of Zarir and other heroes, attention turned increasingly toward him, and Goshtasp realized that continuing the war with Turan would be difficult without Esfandiyar’s strength.

The war between Iran and Turan took on a long and exhausting character. Every victory came with a new wound, and every defeat revealed the need for another champion. The Turanians also possessed great warriors, and Arjasp was not easily driven back. As a result, the frontier between the two countries repeatedly became a battlefield.

But the importance of this war lies not only in the outcome of its battles. With Zarir’s death and Esfandiyar’s emergence, a new generation of the epic enters the center of the story. From this point onward, Esfandiyar will be not merely a young prince but one of the principal pillars of Iran’s defense—a champion whose fate will eventually place him before his father’s most difficult command: to confront Rustam.

29.title: Part 29: Esfandiyar’s Seven Labors
29.prose:
To free his daughters Homay and Beh-Afarid, who were imprisoned in the Turanian fortress of Ruyin-Dezh, Goshtasp sent Esfandiyar on a difficult journey. On the surface, the mission was an opportunity to prove his valor, but beneath it lay the continuing conflict between father and son: Goshtasp had a great champion before him, yet still feared making him his successor. Esfandiyar was forced to enter a land whose passage was far from easy.

Esfandiyar set out from Iran with an army, but he did not choose the direct route. Instead he passed through the path that the Shahnameh made famous as the Seven Labors. Each labor was a separate trial, confronting the champion with a new danger. First came the desert, thirst, and the hardship of the journey; then wild beasts and enemies lying in wait tested his physical strength and resolve. In one of the labors, wolves, lions, and powerful creatures blocked his path, and Esfandiyar passed them through strength and endurance.

Later, a fearsome dragon blocked the road. The struggle was not merely a test of power; it required awareness and timing. Through wisdom and courage, Esfandiyar overcame this danger as well. He then encountered a sorceress who tried to turn him from his path through deception and trickery. Esfandiyar was not deceived by appearances and recognized the truth of the enemy. After that, the road toward the enemy’s land opened further, and through perseverance and command he brought his army close to Ruyin-Dezh.

Esfandiyar’s Seven Labors are not merely a collection of heroic battles. In this journey he becomes more fully known as a champion who possesses both martial strength and the ability to decide in moments of danger. He emerges from each labor with new experience and moves toward a fortress where freeing his sisters and breaking the enemy’s power will be the next stage of his mission. At last Esfandiyar approached Ruyin-Dezh and prepared for the battle that would place his name among the greatest champions of the new generation.

30.title: Part 30: The Opening of the Invulnerable Fortress
30.prose:
After passing the Seven Labors, Esfandiyar reached Turan and made his way to the Invulnerable Fortress, a stronghold renowned for its strength and impenetrability, which for years had kept enemies from approaching. Inside the fortress, Homay and Beh-Afarid, Esfandiyar’s sisters, were held captive, and freeing them was one of the chief aims of his campaign.

Esfandiyar knew that a direct assault could inflict heavy losses on the Iranian army. Before beginning the battle, therefore, he turned to strategy and careful planning. He sought a way to approach the fortress and, at last, through a suitable disguise and a calculated plan, found a means of entering its walls. This part of the story shows that heroism is not merely a matter of physical strength: sometimes victory comes through wisdom and an understanding of circumstances.

Once the way was opened, fighting began inside the Invulnerable Fortress. Its defenders fought with all their strength, but Esfandiyar and his army overcame them. The walls that had for years been a symbol of the enemy’s security fell before the Iranian hero’s resolve, and the fortress finally came into Iranian hands. After his victory, Esfandiyar found his sisters and freed them from captivity.

Homay and Beh-Afarid left the fortress with the Iranian army, and Esfandiyar, having fulfilled his mission, prepared to return. The victory further strengthened his standing among Iran’s heroes: he had survived the Seven Labors and, through strategy and courage, opened a fortress whose conquest had seemed nearly impossible.

Yet his victorious return did not end Esfandiyar’s troubles. He hoped that after all these services, Goshtasp would keep his promise and give him the royal crown. Instead, his father once again placed a difficult task before him. Thus the victory at the Invulnerable Fortress became the beginning of a darker stage, one that would ultimately send Esfandiyar toward Zabul and his confrontation with Rustam.

31.title: Part 31: Arjasp and the End of the Great War
31.prose:
After the opening of the Invulnerable Fortress, the conflict between Iran and Turan was still not over. Arjasp, unwilling to accept his repeated defeats, once again began thinking of gathering his forces and returning to the battlefield. Goshtasp also knew that the enemy still had the capacity to attack and that the Iranian army had to be prepared for another war.

Another battle broke out, and the two armies drew up against one another. In this battle, Esfandiyar was no longer merely a young man seeking fame; the experience of the Seven Labors and his victory at the Invulnerable Fortress had made him one of the Iranian army’s principal hopes. He fought beside the other heroes and carried the heavy burden of defending the country.

The fighting was fierce and costly. Many soldiers fell on the field, and every victory came with suffering and the loss of many lives. Nevertheless, Iran’s forces eventually defeated the Turanian army, and Arjasp was forced to retreat and flee. His defeat brought one of the greatest wars of this period to an end and, for a time, pushed the direct Turanian threat away from Iran’s borders.

Yet behind this victory, another matter remained unresolved. Esfandiyar expected Goshtasp, after years of service and difficult commands, to fulfill his promise of the kingship. Instead of reassuring his son, Goshtasp remained afraid of his power and popularity. Thus the end of the war did not mean the end of the conflict between father and son.

On one side, Esfandiyar was a victorious and beloved hero; on the other, he faced a father who repeatedly postponed his arrival on the throne to an uncertain future. This struggle would eventually lead Goshtasp to issue a new command: Esfandiyar was to be sent to Zabul, where Iran’s two great heroes, Esfandiyar and Rustam, would be set against one another. From here the story moves from war with an external enemy toward a tragedy within the royal and heroic family.

32.title: Part 32: Rustam and Esfandiyar — The Difficult Command
32.prose:
After years of war and heroism, Esfandiyar believed the time had come for Goshtasp to keep his promise and hand the royal crown to him. He had fought many battles for his father and his country, passed through the Seven Labors, and opened the Invulnerable Fortress; he expected now to receive the reward for all those services. But Goshtasp once again refused his request and placed a new mission before him.

The king’s command was that Esfandiyar go to Zabulistan and bring Rustam, Iran’s greatest hero, before him in chains. For Esfandiyar, this was no simple order. Rustam was not a hero who would easily submit, yet Esfandiyar could not ignore the command of his father and king. At the same time, there was no personal enmity between the two men, and both were among the great figures of Iran.

Esfandiyar traveled toward Zabulistan and delivered Goshtasp’s message to Rustam. Rustam knew his own standing and did not want, after a lifetime of service to Iran, to be taken to court like a prisoner. He said he was willing to go before the king, but that binding his hands and taking him by force was incompatible with a hero’s honor and the name of his family. Rustam tried to find a way to end the dispute through conversation.

Esfandiyar also knew that Rustam was a great and aged hero, and that fighting him could harm Iran. Nevertheless, he saw himself as responsible for obeying the king’s command. He said that if Rustam accepted the order, there would be no bloodshed or war; but if he refused, Esfandiyar would have no choice but to carry out his mission. Thus the two men became trapped between mutual respect and the duty each understood himself to bear.

Rustam again proposed that he go to Goshtasp without being bound and speak with him about the dispute. But Esfandiyar regarded the command as unequivocal and was unwilling to alter it. He said that if he disobeyed the king, he too would be accused of rebellion. Their words led nowhere, and the path of peace was closed.

At last, the confrontation between the two heroes began—not because one was an enemy of Iran and the other its defender, but because of a command that had come from the court. This is what makes their battle different from many other wars in the Shahnameh. Here tragedy begins where two great heroes could have been allies, but royal power and command place them on opposite sides of the field. The battle between Rustam and Esfandiyar now appears unavoidable.

33.title: Part 33: Rustam and Esfandiyar — The Battle of Two Heroes
33.prose:
پس از آنکه گفت‌وگو میان رستم و اسفندیار به نتیجه نرسید، دو پهلوان بزرگ ایران در برابر یکدیگر ایستادند. هر دو می‌دانستند که جنگ با دیگری آسان نیست و هر دو از پیامدهای این رویارویی بیم داشتند، اما فرمان شاه و آبروی پهلوانی راه بازگشت را تنگ کرده بود.

رستم با تجربهٔ سال‌های دراز و نیرویی که از نبردهای بی‌شمار به دست آورده بود، به میدان آمد. اسفندیار نیز جوان‌تر، نیرومند و برخوردار از زرهی بود که او را در برابر بیشتر سلاح‌ها رویین‌تن کرده بود. ضربه‌های رستم بر تن اسفندیار کارگر نمی‌افتاد و تیرها و نیزه‌ها راهی برای نفوذ در زره او پیدا نمی‌کردند.

نبرد طولانی شد و هیچ‌یک به آسانی پیروز نشد. رستم و رخش آسیب دیدند و پهلوان پیر دریافت که نیروی معمولی برای پایان دادن به این کار کافی نیست. او زخمی و خسته نزد زال رفت و از پدر خواست چاره‌ای بیندیشد. زال که خطر را جدی می‌دید، به یاد سیمرغ افتاد؛ همان مرغ افسانه‌ای که از کودکی در سرنوشت خاندان سام حضور داشت.

زال پر سیمرغ را به کار گرفت و سیمرغ فراخوانده شد. سیمرغ رستم و رخش را درمان کرد و پس از شنیدن ماجرای نبرد، راز شکست اسفندیار را آشکار ساخت. بدن اسفندیار در برابر سلاح‌ها آسیب‌ناپذیر بود، اما چشم‌های او از این مصونیت برخوردار نبودند. راه پیروزی، نه زور بیشتر، بلکه شناخت نقطهٔ ضعف پهلوان رویین‌تن بود.

رستم از اینکه باید چنین راهی را برگزیند خشنود نبود. اسفندیار دشمن شخصی او نبود و رستم می‌دانست که جوانی چون او قربانی فرمان پدر و بازی قدرت دربار شده است. با این حال، اگر خود را تسلیم می‌کرد، خاندان و آزادگی‌اش را از دست می‌داد و اگر می‌جنگید، احتمال کشته شدن یکی از دو پهلوان بزرگ ایران وجود داشت.

نبرد دوباره از سر گرفته شد. این بار رستم با دانشی که سیمرغ به او داده بود، تیر ویژه‌ای آماده کرد. لحظه‌ای فرا رسید که اسفندیار در تیررس قرار گرفت و رستم تیر را به سوی چشم او رها کرد. تیر به هدف نشست و اسفندیار، که تا آن لحظه شکست‌ناپذیر می‌نمود، بر زمین افتاد.

اسفندیار در واپسین لحظات دریافت که سرنوشت او بیش از آنکه ساختهٔ دشمنی با رستم باشد، نتیجهٔ فرمانی بود که از سوی پدرش آمده بود. او از رستم خواست مراقب بهمن، پسرش، باشد و آیندهٔ او را فراموش نکند. بدین ترتیب، پیروزی رستم رنگ شادی نداشت؛ زیرا با مرگ اسفندیار، ایران یکی از بزرگ‌ترین پهلوانان نسل تازه را از دست داد و رستم نیز بار دیگر قربانی تصمیم‌های شاهان شد.

34.title: Part 34: The End of Esfandiyar and Bahman
34.prose:
پس از آنکه تیر رستم بر چشم اسفندیار نشست، پهلوان جوان دریافت که زخم او مرگبار است. پایان نبرد برای هیچ‌یک از دو پهلوان با شادی همراه نبود؛ زیرا رستم می‌دانست مردی را از میان برده که دشمن شخصی او نبود و اسفندیار نیز در واپسین لحظه‌ها دریافت که فرمان پدرش او را به چنین سرنوشتی کشانده است.

اسفندیار پیش از مرگ، رستم را سرزنش نکرد و از او خواست به یاد بهمن، پسر جوانش، باشد. او آیندهٔ فرزند خود را به پهلوان بزرگ ایران سپرد و خواست که بهمن راه و رسم پهلوانی را بیاموزد. این درخواست، تلخی نبرد را بیشتر کرد؛ زیرا دو خاندان که در میدان رویاروی هم قرار گرفته بودند، از راه بهمن دوباره به یکدیگر پیوند می‌خوردند.

رستم از مرگ اسفندیار سخت اندوهگین شد. او می‌دانست که اگر فرمان گشتاسپ نبود، این دو پهلوان می‌توانستند در کنار یکدیگر برای ایران بجنگند. از نگاه رستم، گشتاسپ برای حفظ تاج و جلوگیری از قدرت گرفتن پسرش، از فرمان شاهانه استفاده کرده و اسفندیار را به رویارویی با او فرستاده بود.

پس از مرگ اسفندیار، خشم و اندوه در خاندان گشتاسپ بالا گرفت. بهمن که هنوز جوان بود، در میان این کشمکش قرار داشت. رستم به عهد خود وفادار ماند و او را پذیرفت و پرورش داد. بدین ترتیب، بهمن مدتی در زابل و در کنار خاندان سام و زال با آیین پهلوانی آشنا شد و از تجربهٔ رستم بهره برد.

بهمن در وجود خود دو میراث مهم را حمل می‌کرد: از سوی پدر، جایگاه خاندان گشتاسپ و اسفندیار را و از سوی پیوندی که پس از مرگ پدر با رستم پیدا کرد، بخشی از سنت پهلوانی خاندان سام را. همین پیوند نشان می‌داد که حتی در دل دشمنی‌های خونین، شاهنامه راه‌هایی برای انتقال تجربه و میراث از نسلی به نسل دیگر می‌گشاید.

مرگ اسفندیار همچنین نشانهٔ پایان یک دوره بود. او آخرین پهلوان بزرگ نسل خود بود که با فرمان شاه به جنگ پهلوانی هم‌سنگ خویش رفت و در این راه جان باخت. رستم نیز پس از این حادثه بیش از پیش با بار سنگین گذشته و تصمیم‌های شاهان روبه‌رو شد.

از این پس، داستان به سوی نسل‌های تازه و دگرگونی قدرت پیش می‌رود. بهمن، که اکنون تحت حمایت رستم قرار گرفته بود، آینده‌ای متفاوت در پیش داشت و نام اسفندیار از راه او در تاریخ پهلوانی ایران باقی می‌ماند. میراث اسفندیار دیگر تنها خاطرهٔ یک پهلوان رویین‌تن نبود، بلکه در تربیت و سرنوشت فرزندش ادامه پیدا می‌کرد.

35.title: Part 35: Bahman and the Beginning of a New Generation
35.prose:
پس از مرگ اسفندیار، بهمن در میان دو میراث بزرگ رشد کرد. او فرزند پهلوانی بود که در نبردی تلخ به دست رستم کشته شده بود، اما همان رستم به عهد خود وفا کرد و بهمن را پذیرفت و آیین پهلوانی آموخت. از همین رو، کودکی و جوانی بهمن در سایهٔ خاطرهٔ دو پهلوان بزرگ سپری شد و او از هر دو خاندان چیزی برای آینده با خود برد.

بهمن در کنار رستم با رسم جنگاوری، وفاداری، سخن گفتن با بزرگان و شناخت دشواری‌های فرمانروایی آشنا شد. رستم برای او تنها پهلوانی نامدار نبود؛ بلکه آموزگاری بود که می‌توانست تجربهٔ نسل‌های پیشین را به جوانی منتقل کند. این رابطه، زخم میان دو خاندان را از راه یک نسل تازه تا اندازه‌ای به پیوندی انسانی تبدیل کرد.

با گذشت سال‌ها، بهمن به دربار بازگشت و جایگاه خود را در خاندان پدری شناخت. نام اسفندیار همچنان با خاطرهٔ جنگ با رستم همراه بود، اما بهمن مجبور نبود همهٔ دشمنی‌های گذشته را تکرار کند. او می‌توانست میراث پدر را با تجربه‌ای که از رستم گرفته بود درهم آمیزد و راهی تازه برای خود بسازد.

در این دوره، جهان پهلوانی نیز در حال دگرگونی بود. رستم و بسیاری از قهرمانان نسل پیشین دیگر در مرکز همهٔ رویدادها نبودند و قدرت سیاسی بیش از گذشته به خاندان‌های شاهی و نسل‌های تازه منتقل می‌شد. بهمن در چنین زمانی اهمیت پیدا کرد، زیرا میان گذشته و آینده ایستاده بود.

داستان بهمن نشان می‌دهد که میراث پهلوانی فقط از راه خون و نسب منتقل نمی‌شود. گاهی یک جوان می‌تواند از دو سوی یک دشمنی تاریخی تجربه بیاموزد و آن را به شکل دیگری ادامه دهد. بهمن از خاندان اسفندیار بود، اما سال‌هایی از تربیت او در کنار رستم گذشت؛ بنابراین گذشتهٔ متعارض ایران در شخصیت او به هم رسید.

با بازگشت بهمن به جایگاه سیاسی و درباری، مسیر داستان از تراژدی رستم و اسفندیار به دوره‌ای تازه نزدیک شد. دیگر مسئله تنها رویارویی دو پهلوان نبود؛ بلکه پرسش اصلی این بود که پس از پایان نسل بزرگ قهرمانان، چه کسانی بار فرمانروایی و دفاع از ایران را بر دوش خواهند گرفت.

بهمن سرانجام به پادشاهی رسید و نام او در شمار پادشاهان ایران قرار گرفت. دوران او آغاز مرحله‌ای تازه در روایت شاهنامه است؛ مرحله‌ای که در آن پیوند میان قدرت شاهی و میراث پهلوانی شکل دیگری پیدا می‌کند. خاطرهٔ رستم و اسفندیار همچنان باقی است، اما نسل تازه باید سرنوشت خود را رقم بزند.

36.title: Part 36: The Reign of Bahman
36.prose:
After Goshtasp, Bahman ascended the throne of Iran and took upon himself the legacy of his father and grandfather. In childhood and youth, he had lived with the memory of Esfandiyar and had learned the code of the hero from Rustam; his reign therefore stood between two great traditions: royal power and the culture of the champions.

At the beginning of his rule, Bahman sought to strengthen the authority of the government throughout the country. He organized the court and army and worked to secure the borders and consolidate the position of the Kayanian house. Yet the conflicts inherited from the previous generation were still alive, and the relationship between the court and the house of Zal was no longer as simple as before.

Rustam’s name remained bound to Iran’s greatest victories, but his death and then Esfandiyar’s showed that the age of the great heroes was changing. Bahman wanted to emphasize royal authority, and this brought him into tension with the powerful and independent houses of Sistan.

In accounts of this period, Bahman’s severity toward Zal’s family becomes one of the defining features of his reign. He had not forgotten his father’s death and saw a political distance between his own rule and Rustam’s legacy. This conflict was more than a personal enmity; it revealed a rivalry between two centers of power: the royal throne and the heroic house.

Bahman sought to consolidate his authority through armies and royal commands. Yet the Shahnameh shows that political power, however extensive, cannot easily endure without ties to the heroes and great men of the country. His reign therefore became entangled in the same question that had faced earlier generations: the relationship between king and hero.

After years of Bahman’s rule, succession entered a new stage. He had a daughter named Homay, and the story now turns toward her life and that of her son Darab. A new branch of the royal line begins to take shape, and the Shahnameh moves farther away from the heroic age of Sistan.

Bahman’s reign is, overall, a period of transition. On one side, Esfandiyar’s name and the Kayanian tradition remain central; on the other, a new generation of rulers and heroes is emerging. With the passing of Rustam and Esfandiyar’s generation, Iranian history enters a stage in which the throne and royal lineage assume a greater role.

37.title: Part 37: Homay Chehrazad and the Succession of a Woman
37.prose:
After Bahman, Homay Chehrazad took the throne of Iran and ruled for a number of years. Her place among the kings of the Shahnameh shows that the Iranian epic does not restrict authority and wisdom to men. Homay was a woman of judgment and power, able to govern the country while the memory of the great wars was still alive.

Homay belonged to the house of Goshtasp and Esfandiyar, so her succession continued that dynasty. Yet the atmosphere of the story changes in her time. The narrative is no longer centered only on the battles of heroes; the throne, succession, family secrets, and the future of the royal line become increasingly important.

Homay had a son named Darab. But the circumstances of the court and fear of disorder over the succession led her to conceal the child’s fate and separate him from herself. Darab was taken from his mother in childhood, and his life continued along an unknown path. This separation became one of the great secrets of this part of the story.

Years passed, and Darab grew up without fully knowing his true position. His fate gradually drew him toward the army and the court. Signs of his lineage and worth began to appear, until the story reached the point where his ancestry could no longer remain hidden.

Despite the difficult decision she had made about her son, Homay continued to bear the responsibility of kingship. In the Shahnameh, her rule represents a period in which preserving the country’s order and the continuity of the dynasty could require harsh and painful decisions.

Darab’s return to power was not merely a family matter. Once his lineage was revealed, the future of the crown changed again and a new generation of kings emerged. From here the story moves toward Darab and then another Bahman, the king who would later stand against Alexander’s power.

Homay Chehrazad therefore holds a special place in this chain of events: she is both king and mother, and her decision concerning Darab changes the course of succession. Her story shows that sometimes the fate of a dynasty is determined not on the battlefield, but in the silence of a palace and in the decision of a ruler.

38.title: Part 38: Darab and the Return of the Prince
38.prose:
Darab, the son of Homay, was finally recognized as the rightful heir after years away from the court. The signs of royal lineage were evident in him, and his ability and courage showed that he was prepared to rule. Once the secret of his ancestry was revealed, the course of succession changed again, and Darab took the throne of Iran.

At the beginning of his reign, Darab sought to preserve the country’s authority and keep its borders secure against its enemies. His period was marked by campaigns and political confrontations, and Iran’s relations with the lands to the west became increasingly important. From this point, the Shahnameh gradually enters a world in which Iran stands alongside Rome and more distant lands.

Darab fought his enemies to consolidate his power and did not retreat before rebellion or threat. In the epic narrative, his reign forms part of the chain of rulers who must preserve Iran’s inheritance for the next generation. Yet his fate also shows that no king can remain untouched by the great changes of his age.

In Darab’s life, lineage and succession remain crucial. He was the son of a mother who had herself sat upon the throne, and his return to power was the result of years in which the truth had been concealed. His kingship therefore continues the story begun with Homay: the secret of one family can change the future of an entire country.

Darab had a son named Dara, and after him the crown passed to another generation. Dara’s story brings Iran into an age in which contact with the Hellenic world and the name of Alexander move to the center of the narrative. Here the Shahnameh blends Iranian traditions about Alexander with historical and legendary material.

For Ferdowsi, Darab serves largely as a link: on one side he continues the Kayanian dynasty; on the other, he prepares the way for figures who carry the story of Iran from the earlier heroic world into a new age. After him, the central issue is no longer only the war between Iran and Turan, but Iran’s confrontation with western powers and the transformation of the world order.

The end of Darab’s reign begins the stage in which Dara and then Alexander enter the story. With this transition, the Shahnameh approaches one of its great turning points, where legend, history, and cultural memory stand together.

39.title: Part 39: Dara and the Confrontation with Alexander
39.prose:
Dara ascended the throne of Iran after Darab and inherited the dynasty in a difficult age. The world around Iran was changing, and the western powers were drawing closer to its borders. In the Shahnameh, the greatest threat came from Alexander, king of Macedon, who after his vast conquests advanced toward Iran.

At first, messages and negotiations passed between Dara and Alexander, but their dispute over power and territory finally led to war. Dara gathered a great army and sought to stand against the invaders. Iran possessed great numbers, yet on a battlefield numbers alone do not decide the outcome; the coordination of commanders and their loyalty matter as well.

The battles between the two sides were harsh and costly. Alexander advanced with an organized army and concentrated command, while Dara struggled to hold the Iranian forces together.
